name: Water Walk
description: We are hosting our third annual Water Walk on Saturday, March 29th from 1:00pm to 5:00pm. The walk around Swan Lake will begin at the lake side of the Trone Center with a ribbon cutting ceremony at 1:00pm. We are asking for a voluntary donation of $5.00 to participate in the Walk. Participants carry two gallons of water around Swan Lake to mimic what the average woman must do to get her water in the developing world. With hundreds of volunteers carrying water we will raise awareness that access to clean water demands our immediate attention. Donations collected will be used to fund a potable water system for the Sanik-Ya and Chitulul communities in Guatemala. Sanik-Ya and Chitulul are small Mayan villages on the outskirts of the municipality of San Lucas Tolimán in the State of Sololá, Guatemala. Furman has already raised more than $30,000 through the Walk but there is work to do yet! The total cost for the water project is estimated to cost $100,000. The Guatemalan non-profit organization, Agua del Pueblo, will manage the project. The Furman Water Walk is a student-led initiative created to educate and engage the campus community in addressing the challenges of clean water access in the developing world. History Since the annual Water Walk began in 2012, more than 600 students, faculty, staff and members of the local community walked at least one mile with at least two gallons of water. In 2011 and 2013 Furman students traveled to these communities on the Global Sustainability May Experience. Both groups have conducted research on the topics of sustainable development, water and economic inequality. Both student groups also invested manual labor in the potable water project. The 2011 group began the topographical survey of Sanik-Ya and Chitulul. The 2013 group got their hands dirty clearing the path for the water system. Stanford University is partnering with Furman in this effort by offering a sister course and cooperating on the project and resulting research. Furman students will collect data on the economic situation of the town while Stanford students will collect data on public health. How to Donate The Furman Alumni Association has set up this donation link: furmanwaterwalk.org. You can obtain more information about the organization managing the water project at http://peopleswater.org/ Why Walk? Furman students who participated in last year’s walk felt the largest benefit was the next day when she awoke to realize how many of her muscles ached. Women in the developing world have to do this every day! If we are successful, Furman students & faculty will soon have the opportunity to: -Use a living learning lab in the developing world; -Gather baseline data including economic development in the town; -Offer future study away courses to complete the design and construct the water system; -Evaluate the project in terms of: How the money was spent, and the impacts of potable water on the health and economic development The bottom line is that this is just one more example of the importance of engaged learning - one of our cornerstones. Our students will study the issues of provision of potable water in the “real world”. Students will be involved in every aspect of the project from the planning to the design to the construction to the evaluation. We could never duplicate those learning opportunities in the traditional classroom. More Information Agua del Pueblo (AdP), the non-profit managing the instillation of the water project, hosts and sponsors our May-X course on Global Sustainability in Guatemala. AdP does not solely provide potable water. AdP uses the potable water project as a springboard to encourage a more comprehensive community development. AdP has found the communities that build a water project in a participatory manner are more likely to subsequently build schools, clinics and other amenities to their villages. Our students researched the typical time that a woman in the developing world walks for water. Believe it or not, the average is one mile. Thus we asked water walkers to walk at least one mile. In the "real" developing world, women have to make multiple trips. Researching the amount of water used daily is a bit more challenging. The data are very sparse about the amount of water used. In general the further folks have to walk to obtain their water, the less they use. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends 50 liters (13 gallons) per person per day. Folks without a piped water system use far less, again the WHO has found they use ten liters (2.6 gallons) /person/day. Assuming an average family size is six, and a typical size container (which they balance on their heads) of four gallons, a woman would have to make almost four trips per day! Thank you once again for all of your support . I look forward to seeing you on March 29th toting your gallons of water. Please let us know if you have any questions or if I can help in any way. Bruce Clemens

name: Carrie Newcomer in Concert/CLP!
description: Carrie Newcomer has been described as a "prairie mystic" by the Boston Globe, as one who "asks all the right questions" by Rolling Stone, as "a voice as rich as Godiva chocolate" by The Austin Statesman. One of the definitive voices of the heartland and progressive spirituality, In 2009 Carrie released her twelfth album on Rounder Records, Before and After (featuring Mary Chapin Carpenter on the title track). She has toured with Alison Krauss and Nickel Creek recorded Newcomer’s song "I Should’ve Known Better," on their Grammy-winning album, This Side. Boston’s WUMB listed Carrie as one of the 50 most influential songwriters of the past 50 years and Chicago WBEZ listed her as one of the most influential folk artists of the last 25 years. In the fall of 2009 Newcomer was a cultural ambassador to India invited by the American Embassy of India to tour the country performing for Indian audiences and visiting community services organizations. She taught workshops on songwriting, community service, and met and performed with contemporary, traditional and classical Indian musicians. She also visited slum programs for women and children at risk throughout the country of India. She returned with Gary Walters and James Brock to India Sept 2011 as a visiting artist at the Delhi, Mumbai and Chennai International Schools, and again performing for Indian audiences through the American Embassy of India. In the fall of 2011 Carrie released her 15th album, Everything is Everywhere, as a special benefit project for the Interfaith Hunger Initiative on Available Light Records. In August 2011 The Times Music Company released Everything is Everywhere in India. Newcomer is an acclaimed musician who continues to create music from her uniquely spiritual and poignant take on the world. Everything is Everywhere is no exception, beautifully creating a fusion of east and west. Everything is Everywhere highlights Newcomer's ability to blend her rich alto with a poetic lyricism, seamlessly integrating western song form, American roots influences with the haunting sounds of the Indian classical sarod. In Newcomer’s words, "The songs on Everything is Everywhere were written to address what is unique and fascinating about our cultural differences, and yet reach into the common human thread that pulls between us." Carrie was a co-creator of the popular theater production Wilderness Plots state show and PBS Special based on the book by Scott Russell Sanders. Wilderness Plots was nominated for two regional Emmys in 2012 and broadcast nationally on over fifty PBS affiliates. Carrie and her co-creators, Scott Russell Sanders, Krista Detor, Michael White, Tom Roznowski and Tim Grimm were recognized in both house of the Indiana Legislature for Contributions to the Arts. Carrie internationally facilitates workshops and presents keynotes on the topics of songwriting, spirituality and vocation at colleges, universities, and spiritual communities, retreat centers. Newcomer, a Quaker, cuts across secular and spiritual boundaries. In recent years, she has emerged as a respected and recognized artistic voice for the progressive spiritual community. She’s also worked and created presentations with beloved authors, scientists and progressive theologians, Barbara Kingsolver, Jill Bolte Taylor, Phillip Gulley, Marcus Borg, Jim Wallis, Brian McLaren and Scott Russell Sanders. In 2011 and 2012 Carrie joins Parker J. Palmer in events based on his book Healing the Heart of Democracy. In 2012 Carrie will be joining Philip Gulley, Krista Detor, Scott Russell Sanders for a joyful collaboration called Myths, Miracles, Lyrics and Lies. In 2012 she will also be joining progressive social justice theologians Brian McClaren and Marcus Borg for select shows. In June 2012 Carrie Newcomer will be performing in Kenya, Africa as part of the Indiana University AMPATH program and participating in an interfaith celebration in Chulaimbo as part of the Umoja project associated with The Global Interfaith Partnership. "To my mind—a writer’s mind—Carrie Newcomer is much more than a musician. She's a poet, storyteller, snake-charmer, good neighbor, friend and lover, minister of the wide-eyed gospel of hope and grace." — Barbara Kingsolver, author of The Poisonwood Bible, The Bean Trees, and Animal, Vegetable

Barry will present his award-winning multimedia presentation, “60s Rock - When the Music Mattered,” which examines the styles of music that came together in the 1960s. name: "Evening With" Dinner Series hosts Rev. Beth Templeton
description: Rev. Beth Templeton is the director of "Their Eyes Were Opened," the poverty education program of United Ministries, a Greenville-based social service agency aimed at eradicating poverty in Greenville county. Rev. Templeton has spent the past 30 years working for poverty alleviation in Greenville and is the author of "Loving Our Neighbor: A Thoughtful Approach to Helping People in Poverty". Join us as we learn about her vocational journey, life, and work in Greenville. The Vista House hosts Furman faculty or local community members as featured guest in Vista House’s ongoing interview series known as “An Evening with…” This allows a small group of Furman students to engage in frank conversation and sharp dialogue with interesting and interested members of the larger Furman community. Please join us for dinner this week! If you would like to attend this Wednesday 7 pm dinner, please RSVP to amy.canosa@furman.edu.

name: Tie A Love Knot
description: April is Child Abuse Awareness Month and every time a child is picked up by a DSS worker or a Guardian Ad Litem they are given their very own special blanket that is monogramed with the following, "You are Treasured - You are Loved. Students will be assembling "no sew" fleece blankets simply by tying knots around the border of the blanket. Pizza and music will be provided and the goal is to make 100 blankets. Greenville has the highest child abuse rate in South Carolina. Please come join us for this special opportunity to help make a child feel loved.

name: Running Out of Water: Or just another six-point plan to resolve the water crisis?
description: Keynote Address by Peter Rodgers, Harvard professor of Environmental Engineering. Open Q & A following lecture. Part of the Global Issues Forum Spring Series. Prof. Peter Rogers is Gordon McKay Professor of Environmental Engineering and Professor of City Planning in the Division of Engineering and Applied Sciences at Harvard University. He is a member of the Technical Advisory Committee of the Global Water Partnership, recipient of Guggenheim and Twentieth Century Fellowships. He has carried out extensive field and model studies on population, water and energy resources, and environmental problems in Costa Rica, Pakistan, India, China, the Philippines, Bangladesh and, to a lesser extent, in 25 other countries. His most recent work has focused on the relationship between Chinese electric power developments and their impact on global warming.
